description: Synthesis over a curated source shelf (epistemic level a). Loads the disease's source documents + abstracts, synthesises one section per node strictly from the shelf (provenance per paragraph), and the terminal writer assembles + upserts the synthesis into the GL-4 guideline_synthesis table. The anti-hallucination critic backbone (pmid_verify / source_doc_verify / evaluation_check) is wired in GL-ENGINE-2.

nodes.label: Start
nodes.description: Entry point. Receives disease_slug + section spec from the run's initial context.

nodes.label: Load source shelf
nodes.description: Read the curated source documents for the disease and fetch PubMed abstracts for PMID-bearing docs.

nodes.label: Synthesise: Diagnosis
nodes.description: Diagnosis section — synthesised strictly from the shelf.
nodes.prompt:
Synthesise the DIAGNOSIS section of a living clinical guideline for {{ context.initial.disease_name }}, using ONLY the source documents on the shelf below.

Source shelf. Each document has docId, role, title, scope, covers, and its text.
When textSource is "full-text" you are reading the open-access article body, split by
its own section headings (### lines) — quote and cite from it directly. When
textSource is "abstract" you only have the abstract: say less rather than guessing
what the full paper says.
{{ context.gs-shelf.shelf_docs }}

Rules:
- Write one short orienting sentence, then 2-5 paragraphs.
- Every paragraph MUST set source.doc to the docId it is drawn from. When you took it
  from a full-text section, also set source.loc to that section's heading (e.g.
  "§ Histological and genetic characterisation"), so a reader can find the claim in
  the original. Do NOT invent facts beyond the shelf.
- citations may list PMIDs ONLY if that PMID appears on the shelf; otherwise leave empty.
- When a newer shelf document updates an older one on a point, set the paragraph's
  update field (doc = newer docId, note = what changed).

What this section is FOR — read this twice, it is where these summaries usually fail:
- Write what the guideline RECOMMENDS or ADVISES, not what the disease IS. A reader
  who wants to know what fibrous dysplasia is has Wikipedia. They came here to find
  out what should happen next, and what should not.
- Prefer the specific and decision-changing over the general and safe. "Biopsy is
  usually only necessary in unusual or questionable cases" is worth more than three
  paragraphs on mosaic GNAS activation. If the source states a concrete criterion,
  threshold, sequence of investigations or named test, state it.
- State explicitly what is NOT recommended, and where a common approach is wrong or
  can mislead. Those sentences are the ones that change a decision.
- Do NOT restate the disease mechanism (GNAS → Gsα → cAMP), the epidemiology, or the
  definition unless this section is specifically about it. Every section is written
  independently and cannot see the others, so generic background gets repeated five
  times and crowds out the content each section was meant to carry.
- Stop short of drug DOSING and step-by-step operative protocol — those belong in the
  source document, for the specialist reading it. Everything else that helps a family
  or a first-contact clinician decide what to do next belongs here, in plain language.
  ("Patient-level guidance" means no dosing schedules; it does not mean vague.)
- If the shelf genuinely does not cover this section, return no paragraphs. A section
  that says "no source on the shelf covers this" is more useful than filler.
- Focus: how the diagnosis is established (imaging, histopathology, genetic confirmation), and what is and is not recommended at diagnosis.

Before you answer: look at every shelf document whose textSource is "full-text". If more than one has content relevant to this section, draw at least one paragraph from each of them. A section sourced entirely from the single largest document is a failure, not a safe default.

nodes.label: Load claims + cited abstracts
nodes.description: Collect the freshly-synthesised paragraphs (from the section nodes) + the abstracts already fetched by gs-shelf, so the extractor can paraphrase the passage that backs each claim (Feature 4; zero extra PubMed calls).

nodes.label: Extract grounded source paraphrases
nodes.description: Per claim: judge support against the cited abstract and, ONLY when supported, paraphrase the backing passage (1-2 sentences, our own words). Feeds the 'Where we know this from' provenance view.
nodes.prompt:
You are grounding an AI-written clinical synthesis for {{ context.initial.disease_name }}. For each claim below, look ONLY at the abstract of the source it cites — do NOT bring in outside knowledge.

Source abstracts (docId, pmid, title, abstract):
{{ context.gs-quotes-load.sources }}

Claims (each: section_id, paragraph_id, text, cited_doc, cited_pmid, citations):
{{ context.gs-quotes-load.claims }}

For EACH claim return an object with section_id, paragraph_id, a verdict, and a quotes list:
- First decide the verdict: 'supported' = the cited abstract clearly backs the claim; 'unsupported' = it does not back it or contradicts it; 'uncertain' = the abstract is too thin to tell. Be strict: an abstract that does not mention the specific claim is 'uncertain', not 'supported'.
- ONLY when the verdict is 'supported', add one (rarely two) quote(s). Each quote: pmid (a PMID that is in this claim's citations), paraphrase, and optionally supports. If the verdict is 'unsupported' or 'uncertain', return an EMPTY quotes list — that is the correct answer, not a failure.
- The paraphrase MUST be 1-2 short sentences in YOUR OWN WORDS (max ~400 characters). NEVER copy a sentence verbatim from the abstract; summarise it. Stay strictly faithful to the abstract — add no claim the abstract does not make.
- Use ONLY the PMIDs given in that claim's citations. Never invent a PMID and never attribute to a paper not cited by the claim.

nodes.label: Assemble + write synthesis
nodes.description: Collect the section outputs (with grounded paraphrases merged in) and upsert the synthesis into the GL-4 guideline_synthesis table (terminal node).
